explanation: Hydrochloric acid donates H⁺ ions and sodium hydroxide provides OH⁻ ions. The H⁺ and OH⁻ ions combine to form water (H₂O), while the Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions remain in solution as sodium chloride (table salt). This is a classic acid-base neutralization reaction.

safetyWarnings.description: Both HCl and NaOH are corrosive. Wear gloves and goggles.

funFact: This reaction produces ordinary table salt (NaCl) — the same salt you put on your food! Neutralization reactions like this happen in your stomach when you take an antacid.

explanation: Silver ions (Ag⁺) from silver nitrate combine with chloride ions (Cl⁻) from sodium chloride to form insoluble silver chloride, which precipitates out of solution as a white solid. This is a double displacement reaction driven by the formation of an insoluble product.

safetyWarnings.description: Silver nitrate stains skin and clothing black.

funFact: This reaction is used as a test for chloride ions in analytical chemistry. Silver chloride is also light-sensitive, which is why traditional photographic film is coated with silver halides!

observations: Fast and fiery with iron filings or steel wool
explanation: Iron atoms lose electrons (are oxidized) and oxygen molecules gain electrons (are reduced). Each iron atom loses 3 electrons to form Fe³⁺, while each oxygen atom gains 2 electrons to form O²⁻. The ions combine to form iron(III) oxide, commonly known as rust.

safetyWarnings.description: Steel wool burns vigorously in pure oxygen.

funFact: Rusting costs the global economy over $2.5 trillion annually. The Eiffel Tower requires 60 tons of paint every 7 years to protect it from rust!

explanation: Methane undergoes complete combustion in excess oxygen. The carbon in methane is oxidized to carbon dioxide and the hydrogen is oxidized to water. This is a highly exothermic reaction that releases 890 kJ/mol of energy, making methane an excellent fuel.
funFact: Natural gas (mostly methane) provides about 24% of the world's energy. Methane is also a potent greenhouse gas — about 80 times more effective at trapping heat than CO₂ over a 20-year period.

explanation: Copper(II) ions (Cu²⁺) from copper sulfate combine with hydroxide ions (OH⁻) from sodium hydroxide to form insoluble copper(II) hydroxide, a blue gelatinous precipitate. The sodium and sulfate ions remain in solution.

safetyWarnings.description: Copper sulfate is harmful if swallowed and irritating to skin.

funFact: When copper(II) hydroxide is heated, it decomposes to black copper(II) oxide — this color change from blue to black is a visually striking chemistry demonstration.

explanation: Zinc is more reactive than hydrogen in the activity series, so it displaces hydrogen from hydrochloric acid. Zinc atoms are oxidized to Zn²⁺ ions, while H⁺ ions are reduced to H₂ gas. The hydrogen gas escapes as bubbles.

safetyWarnings.description: Hydrogen gas produced is highly flammable. Keep away from flames.

funFact: This reaction was historically used to fill hydrogen balloons. The hydrogen gas produced can be tested with a burning splint — it makes a 'squeaky pop' sound!

observations: Iron nail gets coated with reddish-brown copper
Blue solution gradually turns pale green
explanation: Iron is more reactive than copper in the activity series. Iron atoms lose 2 electrons and are oxidized to Fe²⁺ ions, while Cu²⁺ ions gain those electrons and are reduced to metallic copper, which deposits on the iron surface.

safetyWarnings.description: Copper sulfate is an irritant. Avoid ingestion.

funFact: This reaction was used in ancient China and Spain to extract copper from solution — a process called cementation. It's one of the earliest known examples of applied chemistry!

observations: No visible change in clear solutions
explanation: Sulfuric acid is a diprotic acid, meaning it can donate two H⁺ ions. Each H⁺ combines with an OH⁻ from NaOH to form water. Two moles of NaOH are needed to fully neutralize one mole of H₂SO₄. The Na⁺ and SO₄²⁻ ions form sodium sulfate.
funFact: The heat released in this neutralization can be measured using a calorimeter and is approximately 57.3 kJ/mol per mole of water formed — a constant for strong acid-strong base neutralizations.

explanation: Nitric acid donates H⁺ to sodium hydroxide's OH⁻ forming water. The sodium and nitrate ions form sodium nitrate in solution. This is a typical strong acid-strong base neutralization.

safetyWarnings.description: Nitric acid is a strong oxidizer.

funFact: Sodium nitrate (the product) is historically known as 'Chile saltpeter' and was mined extensively in the Atacama Desert for use in explosives and fertilizers.

observations: CO₂ gas produced turns limewater milky
explanation: The acid reacts with the carbonate ion (CO₃²⁻), which is a base. The carbonic acid formed (H₂CO₃) immediately decomposes into water and carbon dioxide gas. The calcium and chloride ions remain in solution.
funFact: This is the reaction that occurs when acid rain dissolves limestone buildings and statues. It's also how antacid tablets (containing CaCO₃) neutralize excess stomach acid!

explanation: The hydrogen ion from HCl reacts with the bicarbonate ion to form carbonic acid, which immediately decomposes to water and carbon dioxide. The fizzing is caused by the rapid release of CO₂ gas.
funFact: This is essentially what happens inside a baking soda volcano! It's also the reaction in effervescent antacid tablets and in baking when baking soda meets an acidic ingredient.

explanation: Acetic acid (vinegar) reacts with sodium bicarbonate (baking soda). The H⁺ from acetic acid reacts with bicarbonate to form unstable carbonic acid, which decomposes to CO₂ and water. This is actually slightly endothermic — the solution cools down.
funFact: This is the classic 'baking soda and vinegar volcano' reaction! It's one of the most popular science fair experiments and is completely safe to do at home.

observations: Do not look directly at the flame
explanation: Magnesium is oxidized from Mg(0) to Mg²⁺, losing 2 electrons. Oxygen is reduced from O(0) to O²⁻, gaining 2 electrons. The reaction is highly exothermic, producing an intense white light as the magnesium burns. The product is white magnesium oxide powder.

safetyWarnings.description: Do NOT look directly at burning magnesium — it can damage your eyes.
Magnesium burns at very high temperatures and is difficult to extinguish.

funFact: Burning magnesium was used in early camera flash bulbs and is still used in military flares and fireworks. The flame reaches temperatures of about 3,100°C!

observations: Sodium moves rapidly on water surface
explanation: Sodium is highly reactive and readily gives up its single valence electron to water. The sodium is oxidized to Na⁺ while water is reduced, releasing hydrogen gas and forming hydroxide ions. The reaction is so exothermic that with larger pieces of sodium, the hydrogen gas may ignite.

safetyWarnings.description: Larger pieces can explode violently. Use only very small pieces.
Hydrogen gas produced is flammable and may ignite.

funFact: When a larger piece of sodium is thrown into water, it can react so violently that it explodes! Chemistry teachers typically use only tiny pieces (2-3mm) for this demonstration.

observations: Immediately catches fire with lilac/violet flame
explanation: Potassium is even more reactive than sodium. It instantly reacts with water, and the hydrogen gas produced is always ignited by the heat of the reaction. The characteristic lilac flame comes from excited potassium atoms.

safetyWarnings.description: Potassium reacts explosively with water. Extreme caution required.

funFact: Potassium reacts so violently with water that it always catches fire, producing a beautiful lilac/violet flame. This is why alkali metals are stored under mineral oil!

explanation: Zinc is above copper in the reactivity series, so it can displace copper from its salt solution. Zinc atoms are oxidized (Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻), while copper ions are reduced (Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu). The blue color fades as Cu²⁺ ions are removed from solution.
funFact: This reaction demonstrates the principle behind the Daniell cell, one of the first practical batteries invented in 1836 by John Frederic Daniell.

observations: When heated and cooled slowly, golden crystals form (golden rain)
explanation: Lead(II) ions combine with iodide ions to form lead(II) iodide, which is insoluble in cold water and precipitates as a bright yellow solid. This is a classic double displacement (metathesis) reaction.

safetyWarnings.description: Lead compounds are toxic. Avoid skin contact and ingestion.
Lead is a persistent environmental pollutant. Dispose properly.

funFact: The 'Golden Rain' experiment is one of the most beautiful demonstrations in chemistry. When a hot solution of PbI₂ is slowly cooled, shimmering golden-yellow crystals form, resembling falling golden rain!

observations: Burns with a pale blue, almost invisible flame
Water droplets form on cool surfaces
Loud pop if ignited in a test tube
explanation: Hydrogen gas combusts in oxygen to form water. Each hydrogen molecule provides 2 electrons for bonding with oxygen. This is an extremely exothermic reaction (-286 kJ/mol) and is the basis for hydrogen fuel cells.

safetyWarnings.description: Hydrogen-oxygen mixtures (4-75% H₂ in air) are explosive.

funFact: The Hindenburg disaster in 1937 involved the combustion of hydrogen. Today, hydrogen fuel cells use this reaction in a controlled manner to produce electricity for cars and spacecraft!

observations: Burns with a pale blue, nearly invisible flame
explanation: Ethanol undergoes complete combustion in excess oxygen. The carbon atoms are oxidized to CO₂ and the hydrogen atoms are oxidized to H₂O. Ethanol is used as a biofuel because it burns cleanly.

safetyWarnings.description: Ethanol flames can be nearly invisible in daylight.

funFact: Ethanol flames are nearly invisible in daylight, which makes ethanol fires very dangerous in laboratory and racing settings. Some racing teams have learned this the hard way!

explanation: Hydrogen peroxide is thermodynamically unstable and decomposes into water and oxygen. This reaction is slow normally but greatly accelerated by catalysts like manganese dioxide. In biological systems, the enzyme catalase rapidly decomposes H₂O₂ produced during metabolism.

safetyWarnings.description: Hydrogen peroxide is a strong oxidizer at high concentrations.

funFact: The 'Elephant Toothpaste' demonstration uses this reaction with concentrated H₂O₂ and KI catalyst plus dish soap to create a massive foam eruption!

explanation: Aluminum is above hydrogen in the activity series, so it displaces hydrogen from hydrochloric acid. Each aluminum atom loses 3 electrons (Al → Al³⁺ + 3e⁻). The protective oxide layer on aluminum must first be dissolved by the acid before the reaction proceeds vigorously.

safetyWarnings.description: Hydrogen gas is produced and is highly flammable.

funFact: Aluminum foil reacting with drain cleaner (which contains NaOH or HCl) can produce enough hydrogen gas to inflate a balloon — but this is dangerous and should only be done under supervision!

explanation: The carbonate ion reacts with the H⁺ ions from HCl to form carbonic acid (H₂CO₃), which immediately decomposes to water and carbon dioxide gas. Two moles of HCl are needed for each mole of Na₂CO₃.
funFact: This reaction is used in fire extinguishers — the CO₂ produced smothers flames by displacing oxygen.

explanation: This is both a neutralization reaction (acid + base → salt + water) and a precipitation reaction. Barium sulfate is one of the most insoluble salts known, making this reaction essentially irreversible.
funFact: Barium sulfate is so insoluble that it's actually safe to swallow (as a 'barium meal') for X-ray imaging of the digestive tract, even though other barium compounds are toxic!

explanation: Carbon dioxide reacts with calcium hydroxide (limewater) to form insoluble calcium carbonate, which appears as a milky white precipitate. This is the classic test for carbon dioxide gas.
funFact: This reaction is used in the 'limewater test' for CO₂ — one of the most commonly performed tests in school chemistry. Exhaled breath turns limewater milky because it contains about 4% CO₂.

observations: Smoke rings may form in air
explanation: Ammonia gas and hydrogen chloride gas react to form tiny crystals of ammonium chloride, which appear as white smoke. The nitrogen's lone pair accepts a proton (H⁺) from HCl, forming the ammonium ion (NH₄⁺) which pairs with the chloride ion (Cl⁻).

safetyWarnings.description: Both ammonia and HCl gases are toxic and irritating.
The fumes are irritating to eyes and respiratory system.

funFact: This reaction produces dramatic white smoke when ammonia solution is held near concentrated HCl. It was once used as a 'smoke signal' effect in chemistry magic shows!

explanation: Magnesium is a reactive metal that sits above hydrogen in the activity series. It readily gives up its two valence electrons (Mg → Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻), and the H⁺ ions from HCl gain these electrons to form H₂ gas.
funFact: This reaction is so vigorous with magnesium that it's often used in classroom demonstrations. The hydrogen produced can be ignited with a 'squeaky pop' test!

explanation: Iron(III) ions (Fe³⁺) combine with hydroxide ions (OH⁻) to form insoluble iron(III) hydroxide, a rusty brown gelatinous precipitate. This is a typical precipitation reaction and is used to identify Fe³⁺ ions in qualitative analysis.

safetyWarnings.description: NaOH is corrosive. FeCl₃ solution is irritating.

funFact: Iron(III) hydroxide is the main component of rust! The brown color is the same as the rust you see on old cars and iron structures.

observations: Precipitate darkens on exposure to air (oxidizes to Fe(OH)₃)
explanation: Iron(II) ions (Fe²⁺) combine with hydroxide ions to form insoluble iron(II) hydroxide, a green gelatinous precipitate. On exposure to air, Fe²⁺ is oxidized to Fe³⁺, and the precipitate gradually changes from green to brown.
funFact: You can watch chemistry happen in real-time: the green Fe(OH)₂ precipitate slowly turns brown as it oxidizes in air to Fe(OH)₃. This is essentially watching iron 'rust' in fast-forward!

explanation: Barium ions (Ba²⁺) and sulfate ions (SO₄²⁻) combine to form barium sulfate, which is extremely insoluble in water (Ksp = 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁰). The reaction is used as the standard test for sulfate ions.

safetyWarnings.description: Barium chloride is toxic if ingested.

funFact: The precipitate BaSO₄ is so insoluble that it's insoluble even in strong acids — unlike most precipitates. This is why it's used as a definitive test for sulfate ions.

observations: No visible change at room temperature

details: Iron catalyst with potassium hydroxide promoter

explanation: The Haber-Bosch process combines atmospheric nitrogen with hydrogen gas to produce ammonia. The triple bond in N₂ is very strong (945 kJ/mol), requiring extreme conditions and a catalyst to break. The reaction is reversible, so Le Chatelier's principle is applied to maximize yield.

safetyWarnings.description: Industrial process operates at very high pressures.
Ammonia is toxic in high concentrations.

funFact: The Haber-Bosch process is arguably the most important chemical reaction in human history — it feeds nearly half the world's population through fertilizer production. Fritz Haber won the Nobel Prize for this in 1918.

details: Concentrated nitric acid for this equation

explanation: Copper does not react with ordinary acids (HCl, H₂SO₄ dilute) because it's below hydrogen in the activity series. However, nitric acid acts as an oxidizing acid. The NO₃⁻ ion oxidizes copper to Cu²⁺, while nitrogen is reduced from +5 to +4 (forming NO₂).

safetyWarnings.description: Brown NO₂ fumes are highly toxic. Perform only in a fume hood.
Concentrated nitric acid is extremely corrosive.

funFact: This reaction demonstrates that nitric acid is special — it can dissolve copper (and many other metals) that regular acids cannot, because it acts as an oxidizing acid rather than relying on H⁺ ions alone.

explanation: Carbon is oxidized from 0 to +4 oxidation state, while oxygen is reduced from 0 to -2. This is complete combustion of carbon, producing carbon dioxide. With insufficient oxygen, incomplete combustion produces carbon monoxide (CO) instead.

safetyWarnings.description: Carbon can burn at high temperatures.

funFact: This same reaction powers most coal-fired power plants. Coal is primarily carbon, and burning it in air produces CO₂ — a major contributor to climate change.

explanation: Sulfur is oxidized from 0 to +4, while oxygen is reduced from 0 to -2. Sulfur burns with a characteristic blue flame in air, producing sulfur dioxide gas which has a strong, choking odor.

safetyWarnings.description: SO₂ is toxic and irritating. Perform in fume hood.

funFact: Sulfur burns with a beautiful blue flame! In Indonesia's Ijen volcano, sulfur burns at night creating an ethereal 'blue fire' — a popular tourist attraction.

observations: Exothermic reaction continues without further heating
Cannot separate with a magnet (unlike the mixture)
explanation: Iron and sulfur combine in a synthesis reaction to form iron(II) sulfide. Unlike a mixture of iron and sulfur (which can be separated by a magnet), the compound FeS has completely different properties — it's non-magnetic, black, and reacts with acids to produce H₂S gas.

safetyWarnings.description: If FeS contacts acid, toxic H₂S gas is produced.
Reaction is very exothermic once started.

funFact: This is a classic demonstration of the difference between a mixture and a compound. A mixture of iron and sulfur can be separated with a magnet, but once they react, the product (FeS) is non-magnetic!

explanation: Calcium oxide (quicklime) reacts vigorously with water in an exothermic reaction called 'slaking'. The oxide ion (O²⁻) reacts with water to form two hydroxide ions. The heat released can be enough to boil the water.

safetyWarnings.description: Generates intense heat — can cause burns.
Both quicklime and slaked lime are corrosive.

funFact: This reaction generates so much heat that it was used to heat food in self-heating cans! Military MREs (Meals Ready to Eat) use CaO + H₂O heaters to warm food in the field.

observations: No visible change in clear solutions
explanation: A typical strong acid-strong base neutralization. The H⁺ from HCl combines with OH⁻ from KOH to form water, while K⁺ and Cl⁻ form potassium chloride.
funFact: Potassium chloride (the product) is commonly used as a salt substitute for people on low-sodium diets. It tastes salty but with a slightly bitter aftertaste.

explanation: Silver ions combine with bromide ions to form insoluble silver bromide. Like all silver halides, AgBr is light-sensitive and darkens when exposed to light due to photoreduction of Ag⁺ to metallic silver.
funFact: Silver bromide is the light-sensitive compound used in black-and-white photographic film. When light hits AgBr crystals, they decompose to form tiny grains of metallic silver, creating the image!

explanation: Silver ions combine with iodide ions to form insoluble silver iodide. The yellow color of AgI distinguishes it from AgCl (white) and AgBr (pale yellow), making this reaction useful in qualitative analysis.
funFact: Silver iodide is used in cloud seeding to make rain! Its crystal structure is similar to ice, so it acts as a nucleus for ice crystal formation in clouds.

explanation: Chlorine undergoes disproportionation — it is simultaneously oxidized and reduced. One Cl atom is reduced from 0 to -1 (in NaCl), while another is oxidized from 0 to +1 (in NaClO). This produces household bleach.
funFact: This is how household bleach (sodium hypochlorite solution) is manufactured! The product NaClO is the active ingredient in Clorox and similar bleach products.

explanation: Calcium ions combine with carbonate ions to form insoluble calcium carbonate, which precipitates as a white solid. This is the same compound found in limestone, chalk, and marble.
funFact: This reaction is essentially how stalactites and stalagmites form in caves — calcium carbonate precipitating from solution over thousands of years!

observations: White suspension clears as Mg(OH)₂ dissolves
explanation: Magnesium hydroxide neutralizes the acid by accepting H⁺ ions. The insoluble Mg(OH)₂ dissolves as it reacts. This is the same reaction that occurs when you take Milk of Magnesia as an antacid.
funFact: This is exactly what happens in your stomach when you take Milk of Magnesia! The Mg(OH)₂ neutralizes excess stomach acid (HCl), providing relief from heartburn.

explanation: Zinc displaces hydrogen from dilute sulfuric acid because zinc is more reactive than hydrogen. The zinc is oxidized to Zn²⁺ and hydrogen ions are reduced to H₂ gas.
funFact: This reaction was one of the ways hydrogen gas was first isolated in the 18th century by Henry Cavendish, who called it 'inflammable air'.

explanation: Concentrated sulfuric acid, being a less volatile acid, displaces the more volatile HCl gas from sodium chloride on heating. This is a classic preparation method for hydrogen chloride gas.

safetyWarnings.description: HCl gas is corrosive and toxic.

funFact: This was historically the main method for producing hydrochloric acid, discovered by Jabir ibn Hayyan (Geber) around 800 CE. The process was later industrialized as the Leblanc process.

observations: Gas turns damp red litmus blue
explanation: When heated with a strong base, the ammonium ion (NH₄⁺) releases ammonia gas. The hydroxide ion deprotonates the ammonium ion. This is the standard lab preparation and test for ammonium ions.

safetyWarnings.description: Ammonia gas is irritating and toxic at high concentrations.

funFact: This reaction is used as the test for ammonium ions in qualitative analysis. If you add NaOH and heat, and the gas produced turns damp red litmus paper blue, ammonium ions are present!

explanation: Iron is more reactive than copper. Iron atoms donate electrons to copper ions, depositing metallic copper. This reaction illustrates the activity series concept.

safetyWarnings.description: Copper sulfate solution is an irritant.

funFact: You can try this at home! Place an iron nail in blue CuSO₄ solution and watch it slowly turn copper-colored over a few hours.

explanation: Zinc ions combine with hydroxide ions to form insoluble zinc hydroxide. Importantly, zinc hydroxide is amphoteric — it dissolves in both excess acid AND excess base. In excess NaOH, it forms the zincate ion [Zn(OH)₄]²⁻.
funFact: Zinc hydroxide demonstrates amphoteric behavior beautifully — add NaOH drop by drop to ZnSO₄ and a precipitate forms. Keep adding NaOH and the precipitate redissolves! This happens because zinc is amphoteric.

explanation: Acetic acid (a weak acid) is neutralized by sodium hydroxide (a strong base). The acetate ion (CH₃COO⁻) is the conjugate base of acetic acid. The resulting sodium acetate solution is slightly basic due to hydrolysis of the acetate ion.
funFact: Sodium acetate is used in 'hot ice' — a supersaturated solution that crystallizes dramatically when triggered, releasing heat. It's the chemistry behind reusable hand warmers!

explanation: Barium ions and sulfate ions combine to form extremely insoluble barium sulfate. This reaction is used as a confirmatory test for sulfate ions in solution.
funFact: BaSO₄ is one of the most insoluble compounds known — its solubility product is about 10⁻¹⁰, meaning virtually none of it dissolves!

explanation: Copper(II) ions combine with sulfide ions to form extremely insoluble copper(II) sulfide, a black precipitate. This reaction is used in qualitative analysis to detect copper ions.

safetyWarnings.description: H₂S is extremely toxic — can be lethal at high concentrations.

funFact: H₂S was historically used in systematic qualitative analysis to separate metal ions into groups. Different metal sulfides have different colors: CuS (black), CdS (yellow), As₂S₃ (yellow), PbS (black).

observations: Less violent than Na/K with water
explanation: Calcium is reactive enough to displace hydrogen from water, though less vigorously than sodium or potassium. Calcium is oxidized to Ca²⁺ while water is reduced, releasing hydrogen gas.
funFact: Unlike sodium and potassium, calcium sinks in water (density 1.55 g/cm³) and reacts more gently, making it a safer demonstration of metal-water reactivity.

explanation: When bleach (NaClO) is mixed with acid, chlorine gas is produced. The Cl⁻ from HCl is oxidized while the Cl⁺ in NaClO is reduced, both forming Cl₂ gas. This is extremely dangerous!

safetyWarnings.description: NEVER mix bleach with acid! Produces deadly chlorine gas.
All reagents and products are hazardous.

funFact: NEVER mix bleach with toilet bowl cleaner or any acid! This common household accident produces chlorine gas, which was used as a chemical weapon in World War I. Call poison control immediately if this happens.

explanation: Phosphoric acid is a triprotic acid — it has three H⁺ ions to donate. Complete neutralization requires 3 moles of NaOH per mole of H₃PO₄. The product is trisodium phosphate (TSP).
funFact: Trisodium phosphate (TSP) was once a common ingredient in laundry detergents and dishwasher powders. It was phased out due to environmental concerns about phosphate pollution causing algal blooms.

observations: Starch indicator turns blue-black if added
explanation: Bromine is more reactive than iodine (higher in the halogen activity series), so it displaces iodine from potassium iodide. Bromine is reduced (Br₂ → 2Br⁻) while iodide is oxidized (2I⁻ → I₂).

safetyWarnings.description: Bromine is highly corrosive and toxic.
Bromine vapors are dangerous. Use in fume hood.

funFact: This reaction demonstrates the halogen displacement series: F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂. Each halogen can displace those below it from their salt solutions, but not those above it.

explanation: Chlorine is more reactive than iodine and displaces it from potassium iodide. Chlorine is reduced to chloride ions while iodide is oxidized to iodine.

safetyWarnings.description: Chlorine gas is highly toxic. Work in fume hood.

funFact: This is a key reaction in water treatment — chlorine is added to water supplies, and any iodide present is oxidized. The starch-iodide test can detect chlorine in water.

explanation: Barium ions combine with sulfate ions to form the highly insoluble barium sulfate precipitate. This is the standard confirmatory test for sulfate ions.
funFact: Barium sulfate is used as a radiocontrast agent in medical imaging. Patients drink a 'barium meal' before X-rays of the digestive system because BaSO₄ is opaque to X-rays.

observations: Clear blue-green solution becomes less colored
explanation: Copper(II) ions combine with hydroxide ions to form insoluble copper(II) hydroxide. This is a characteristic blue precipitate used to identify Cu²⁺ ions.
funFact: This reaction is the basis of the Biuret test for proteins — Cu(OH)₂ reacts with peptide bonds to produce a violet color, confirming the presence of proteins.

explanation: MnO₂ oxidizes HCl. Mn is reduced from +4 to +2, while Cl is oxidized from -1 to 0 (Cl₂). This is a classic lab preparation of chlorine gas. Only 2 of the 4 HCl molecules are oxidized.

safetyWarnings.description: Chlorine gas is extremely toxic. Perform only in fume hood.

funFact: This was the original method Carl Wilhelm Scheele used to discover chlorine in 1774. He called it 'dephlogisticated muriatic acid air' — quite a mouthful compared to 'chlorine'!

explanation: Thiosulfate reacts with acid to form thiosulfuric acid, which is unstable and decomposes. The sulfur in thiosulfate disproportionates — one S is oxidized to SO₂ (+4) and the other is reduced to elemental S (0).

safetyWarnings.description: SO₂ gas is produced — work in ventilated area.

funFact: This reaction is used in the classic 'disappearing cross' rate of reaction experiment! A paper cross is placed under the beaker, and students time how long it takes for the sulfur precipitate to obscure the cross at different temperatures.

explanation: Propane undergoes complete combustion in excess oxygen. All carbon is converted to CO₂ and all hydrogen to H₂O. This reaction releases about 2220 kJ/mol of energy.

safetyWarnings.description: Propane is extremely flammable and explosive in air.

funFact: Propane is the fuel used in most gas barbecue grills. When you grill, you're performing combustion chemistry! About 91.5% of the energy content of propane is released as heat.

explanation: Lithium, the least reactive of the common alkali metals, reacts gently with water. It is oxidized to Li⁺, and water is reduced, releasing hydrogen gas. The reaction is less vigorous than sodium or potassium with water.
funFact: Lithium is the lightest metal (density 0.534 g/cm³) and is one of only three elements that floats on water — along with sodium and potassium. But unlike Na and K, it reacts gently enough to observe safely!

explanation: The thermite reaction is a dramatic displacement reaction. Aluminum is a stronger reducing agent than iron, so it reduces iron(III) oxide to metallic iron. The reaction is so exothermic that the iron is produced in a molten state at about 2500°C.

safetyWarnings.description: Temperature exceeds 2500°C. Can melt through steel.
DO NOT look directly at the reaction.
Produces molten iron — severe burn risk.

funFact: The thermite reaction is used industrially to weld railroad tracks together! The molten iron produced fills the gap between rails and solidifies, creating a strong joint. It was patented in 1895 by Hans Goldschmidt.

explanation: Hydrogen peroxide oxidizes iodide ions (I⁻) to iodine (I₂), while being reduced to water/OH⁻. KI also acts as a catalyst for H₂O₂ decomposition, making this the basis of the Elephant Toothpaste demonstration when soap is added.

safetyWarnings.description: Concentrated H₂O₂ is a strong oxidizer.

funFact: Add dish soap and food coloring to this reaction and you get 'Elephant Toothpaste' — a massive foam eruption that's one of the most popular chemistry demonstrations on the internet!
